claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Verdikt and Allard, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are naïve PSCs that are functionally equivalent to the inner cell mass (ICM) of the E3.5 preimplantation mouse blastocyst.
claims.source: For instance, mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are naïve PSCs that are functionally equivalent to the inner cell mass (ICM) of the E3.5 preimplantation mouse blastocyst (Nichols and Smith, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Nichols and Smith, 2009.

claims.claim: The extended developmental potential of mouse ESCs is associated with their metabolic bivalence.
claims.source: The extended developmental potential of mouse ESCs is associated with their metabolic bivalence, as these cells rely on both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation for energy production.
claims.evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about ESC metabolism.

claims.claim: Differentiation of naïve ESCs into primed PSCs such as epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs) is accompanied by a metabolic shift towards aerobic glycolysis.
claims.source: Differentiation of naïve ESCs into primed PSCs such as epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs) is accompanied by an important metabolic shift towards aerobic glycolysis, in link with a highly proliferative phenotype and a more restricted developmental potential (Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Primordial germ cells (PGCs) are the embryonic precursors of gametes in metazoans.
claims.source: Primordial germ cells (PGCs), the embryonic precursors of gametes in metazoans (Hayashi et al., 2007; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018), are considered dormant totipotent cells because they possess the unique ability to reacquire totipotency upon fertilization (Hayashi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2007; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018.

claims.claim: PGCs possess the unique ability to reacquire totipotency upon fertilization.
claims.source: Primordial germ cells (PGCs), the embryonic precursors of gametes in metazoans (Hayashi et al., 2007; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018), are considered dormant totipotent cells because they possess the unique ability to reacquire totipotency upon fertilization (Hayashi et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Hayashi et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In the mouse embryo, the precursors to PGCs arise around embryonic day 6.25 (E6.25) from formative pluripotent cells in the epiblast.
claims.source: In the mouse embryo, the precursors to PGCs arise around embryonic day 6.25 (E6.25) from formative pluripotent cells in the epiblast (Kinoshita et al., 2021; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Kinoshita et al., 2021; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018.

claims.claim: Progressive increase in oxidative phosphorylation correlates with the specification and differentiation from epiblast PSCs towards PGCs.
claims.source: Progressive increase in oxidative phosphorylation correlates with the specification and differentiation from epiblast PSCs towards PGCs, a process that can be replicated in vitro by inducing PGC-like cells (PGCLCs) from EpiLCs (Hayashi et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The extensive metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic reprogramming that PGCs undergo during their development has been proposed to be uniquely sensitive to environmental insults.
claims.source: In particular, the extensive metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic reprogramming that PGCs undergo during their development has been proposed to be uniquely sensitive to environmental insults, with potential consequences in the offspring (Verdikt et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Verdikt et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The viability of ESCs exposed to Δ9-THC was not significantly altered until the maximal dose of 100 µM.
claims.source: The viability of ESCs exposed to increasing concentrations of Δ9-THC for 48 hr was not significantly altered until the maximal dose of 100 µM, subsequently serving as a positive control, at which only 13.17% of cells remained alive (Figure 1B, p=5.10–15, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The number of viable ESCs significantly increased at doses between 10 nM and 1 µM of Δ9-THC.
claims.source: While no significant changes in viability were observed between 10 nM and 1 µM Δ9-THC, the number of viable ESCs significantly increased by 1.69, 1.52 and 1.28-fold, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 1C, p=0.002, p=0.01 and p=0.03 for 10 nM, 100 nM and 1 µM of Δ9-THC, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The number of viable ESCs significantly increased at doses of Δ9-THC as low as 1 nM.
claims.source: Of note, the number of viable ESCs significantly increased for doses of Δ9-THC as low as 1 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and, 0.59-fold increase, p=0.0005, unpaired T-test), corresponding to doses found in users of 'light cannabis' products (Pacifici et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Pacifici et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The percentage of BrdU-positive ESCs significantly increased between 10 nM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC.
claims.source: The percentage of BrdU-positive ESCs significantly increased between 10 nM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 1D, p=0.01, p=0.001, p=0.05 and p=0.01 for 10 nM, 100 nM, 1 µM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, a significantly higher proportion of ESCs were in the G2/M phase.
claims.source: Co-staining with DAPI (4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) to analyze the cell cycle showed that, at 100 nM of Δ9-THC, a significantly higher proportion of cells were in the G2/M phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and, 0.76-fold increase, p=0.02, unpaired T-test), consistent with cellular proliferation.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The proliferative effect of Δ9-THC exposure on ESCs is sex-independent.
claims.source: Finally, whereas the present data was obtained using female ESCs, the proliferative effect of Δ9-THC exposure on ESCs was also observed in male ESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that proliferation is sex-independent.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly alter cellular viability until the dose of 100 µM.
claims.source: Akin to ESCs, Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly alter cellular viability until the dose of 100 µM (Figure 1E, 11.56% of viable cells, p=1.6–13, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly increase the number of viable cells or the percentage of BrdU-positive cells.
claims.source: However, contrary to ESCs, Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly increase the number of viable cells nor the percentage of BrdU-positive cells (Figure 1F and Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claims.claim: At 10 µM of Δ9-THC, viable EpiLCs numbers and BrdU-positive EpiLCs decreased compared to the mock-treated condition.
claims.source: For the dose of 10 µM of Δ9-THC, viable EpiLCs numbers and BrdU-positive EpiLCs decreased compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 1F, 1.53-fold decrease, p=0.0007, Figure 1G, 1.42-fold decrease, p=0.0024, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) resemble a primed pluripotent state, akin to mouse EpiLCs.
claims.source: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) differ from their murine counterparts, particularly because they resemble a primed pluripotent state, akin to mouse EpiLCs (Weinberger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Weinberger et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Cell viability of hESCs continuously exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC was not significantly impacted.
claims.source: Cell viability of hESCS continuously exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC was not significantly impacted (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: hESCs number was significantly decreased upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: However, hESCs number was significantly decreased upon Δ9-THC exposure (Figure 1—figure supplements 4B and 1.26-fold decrease, p=0.004, unpaired T-test), in a similar trend as observed with mouse EpiLCs (Figure 1E and Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: CB1 was expressed at the same levels at the cell surface of both ESCs and EpiLCs.
claims.source: Western-blot analysis of membrane proteins revealed however that CB1 was expressed at the same levels at the cell surface of both ESCs and EpiLCs (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: Rimonabant pre-treatment abolished Δ9-THC-induced ESCs increased cell number at 100 nM Δ9-THC.
claims.source: Rimonabant pre-treatment did not significantly alter the viability of ESCs compared to conditions exposed to Δ9-THC only (Figure 2C) but abolished Δ9-THC-induced ESCs increased cell number at 100 nM Δ9-THC (Figure 2D, 1.53-fold decrease, p=1.66–05, when comparing 100 nM of Δ9-THC+/-1 µM of SR141716, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: SR141716 pre-treatment reduced ESC cell number compared to control, suggesting a basal role for CB1 in promoting proliferation.
claims.source: Notably, SR141716 pre-treatment, while not altering cell viability, reduced cell number compared to control, suggesting a basal role for CB1 in promoting proliferation.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from the observed reduction in cell number.

claims.claim: The ratio of NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H significantly increased in ESCs at doses between 10 nM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC.
claims.source: In ESCs, the ratio of NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H significantly increased 1.57, 1.54, 1.29, and 1.38 -fold, for 10 nM, 100 nM, 1 µM, and 10 µM of Δ9-THC, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 3B, p=2.87–06, p=8.01–05, p=0.03, and p=0.0003 for 10 nM, 100 nM, 1 µM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: No significant increase was observed in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios in exposed EpiLCs.
claims.source: In contrast, no significant increase was observed in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios in exposed EpiLCs (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios significantly decreased at 10 µM of Δ9-THC in EpiLCs.
claims.source: Consistent with the impact of continuous Δ9-THC exposure on EpiLCs viability (Figure 1H), the NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios significantly decreased at 10 µM of Δ9-THC in EpiLCs (Figure 3B, 59% decrease for 10 µM of Δ9-THC compared to the mock-treated condition, p=6.55–09, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios were slightly but significantly decreased at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in hESCs.
claims.source: Of note, the NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios were slightly but significantly decreased at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in hESCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, 0.09-fold decrease, p=0.04, unpaired T-test), in agreement with the deleterious effect of Δ9-THC on cell number (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A significant increase in mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) associated with the mitochondrial stain was observed at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in ESCs.
claims.source: A significant increase in mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) associated with the mitochondrial stain was observed at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in ESCs (Figure 3C, p=0.02, unpaired T-test), indicating that, at this dose, the observed increase in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H could be explained by higher mitochondrial membrane potential.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: No change in EpiLCs' mitochondrial activity was detected upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: By contrast, no change in EpiLCs' mitochondrial activity was detected (Figure 3C), consistent with these cells relying on glycolysis for energy production (Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021.

claims.claim: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal glycolytic capacity of both ESCs and EpiLCs increased significantly.
claims.source: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal glycolytic capacity of both ESCs and EpiLCs increased significantly (Figure 3D, 15% increase, p=0.03 and 22% increase, p=0.03 for ESCs and EpiLCs, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: A significant decrease in glycolytic capacity was observed at 10 µM of Δ9-THC in both ESCs and EpiLCs.
claims.source: In both cell types, a significant decrease in glycolytic capacity was observed at 10 µM of Δ9-THC (Figure 3D, 39.8% reduction, p=0.0006 and 44.8% reduction, p=0.0001, for ESCs and EpiLCs, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The maximal glycolytic capacity of EpiLCs in the untreated condition was higher than that of ESCs.
claims.source: Of note, the maximal glycolytic capacity of EpiLCs in the untreated condition was higher than the one of ESCs, in agreement with their metabolic shift towards aerobic glycolysis (Figure 3D, 7.88% higher ECAR rate in mock-treated EpiLCs compared to mock-treated ESCs, p=0.03, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs was significantly increased compared to the mock-treated condition.
claims.source: In addition, at 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs was significantly increased compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 3E, 21.8% increase, p=0.03, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The increase in maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs at 100 nM Δ9-THC was observed only for maximal capacity, not for basal or ATP-linked respiration.
claims.source: This increase was observed only for the maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs, but not for basal respiration, nor for ATP-linked respiration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that Δ9-THC impact on mitochondrial respiration does not support increased energetic production.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Increasing doses of Δ9-THC did not alter the maximal respiratory capacity of EpiLCs.
claims.source: In agreement with EpiLCs' metabolic shift towards a glycolytic phenotype, increasing doses of Δ9-THC did not alter their maximal respiratory capacity (Figure 3E), nor their global oxygen consumption rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Of the 126 metabolites detected in ESCs, 39 were significantly upregulated upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: Of the 126 metabolites detected in ESCs, 39 were significantly upregulated (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and only two metabolites – NAPDH and Adenine – were significantly downregulated.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Of the 138 metabolites detected in EpiLCs, 95 were significantly upregulated upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: Of the 138 metabolites detected in EpiLCs, 95 were significantly upregulated (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and only one metabolite – NAPDH – was significantly downregulated.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Pyruvate metabolism and glycolysis were upregulated in both ESCs and EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: Indeed, amongst the 25 metabolic pathways upregulated, pyruvate metabolism and glycolysis were detected in both ESCs and EpiLCs (Figure 4D and Figure 4E, respectively).
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics pathway analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Increased mitochondrial respiration was seen in ESCs with the enrichment of (ubi)quinone metabolism.
claims.source: Increased mitochondrial respiration was also seen in ESCs with the enrichment of (ubi)quinone metabolism, indicating an increased synthesis of ubiquinone that serves as an electron carrier in oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics pathway analysis and inference about ubiquinone function.

claims.claim: The ratio of glutathione in its reduced to oxidized form (GSH/GSSG) was unchanged in both stem cell types in response to Δ9-THC.
claims.source: Of note, metabolite measurements showed that the ratio of glutathione in its reduced to oxidated form (GSH/GSSG) was unchanged in both stem cell types in response to Δ9-THC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the increased mitochondrial respiration does not cause an overt elevation of oxidative stress.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Δ9-THC exposure elicited an increase in metabolic pathways that feed anabolic reactions in both ESCs and EpiLCs.
claims.source: Importantly, and in agreement with the PCA, in both ESCs and EpiLCs, Δ9-THC exposure elicited an increase in metabolic pathways that feed anabolic reactions, in particular contributing to the synthesis of amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan, arginine, alanine, valine, (iso)leucine, etc.), nucleotides ('Pyrimidine metabolism', 'Purine metabolism'), NAD(P)+ ('Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism') and fatty acids ('Butanoate metabolism'; Figure 4D and Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolomics pathway analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Inhibition of glycolysis by 2-DG abrogated the Δ9-THC-induced increase in both ESC cell number and NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H levels.
claims.source: Importantly, glycolytic inhibition by 2-DG abrogated the Δ9-THC-induced increase in both cell number and NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H levels (Figure 4G and Figure 4H, 1.39-fold reduction and p=5.56–05 and 1.68-fold reduction and p=0.0064, respectively, when comparing 100 nM of Δ9-THC+/-10 mM 2-DG, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Exposure to Δ9-THC increases anabolism in both ESCs and EpiLCs, but this increased anabolism only supports cellular proliferation in ESCs.
claims.source: Thus, exposure to Δ9-THC increases anabolism in both ESCs and EpiLCs, however, this increased anabolism only supports cellular proliferation in ESCs.
claims.evidence: Supported by integration of metabolomics and proliferation data.

claims.claim: The vast majority of data variation in transcriptome analysis could be attributed to the cell type rather than to Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: Unsupervised exploration of the global transcriptome by PCA revealed that the vast majority of data variation could be attributed to the cell type (PC1, accounting for 98% of the variation) rather than to Δ9-THC exposure (PC2, accounting for 1% of the variation, Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Δ9-THC exposure does not appear to influence the differentiation dynamics from ESCs to EpiLCs.
claims.source: In addition, mining for the expression of pluripotency markers after Δ9-THC exposure suggested that Δ9-THC does not appear to influence the differentiation dynamics from ESCs to EpiLCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Δ9-THC exposure only moderately impacts ESC and EpiLC transcriptomes.
claims.source: We identified a low number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in both ESCs and EpiLCs (Figure 5C and Figure 5D, respectively), indicating that Δ9-THC exposure only moderately impacts ESC and EpiLC transcriptomes.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5D.

claims.claim: In ESCs, only 12 genes were significantly upregulated with a log2(fold-change) >0.5 and only 9 were significantly downregulated at the same threshold upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: In ESCs, only 12 genes were significantly upregulated with a log2(fold-change) >0.5 and only 9 were significantly downregulated at the same threshold (Figure 5C, significance corresponds to adjusted P-value ≤0.05).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: GO terms associated with metabolic pathways involved in anabolism were significantly over-represented for upregulated genes in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: In particular, GO terms associated with metabolic pathways involved in anabolism were significantly over-represented for upregulated genes in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure (Figure 5E), such as: 'Cellular aromatic compound metabolic process', 'Cellular nitrogen compound biosynthetic process', 'Organonitrogen compound metabolic process'.
claims.evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: GO terms associated with metabolism were not found within the upregulated DEGs in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: In contrast, GO terms associated with metabolism were not found within the upregulated DEGs in EpiLCs.
claims.evidence: Supported by GO analysis results.

claims.claim: Several GO terms relating to alterations in cellular components were enriched in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: However, several GO terms relating to alterations in cellular components were enriched in EpiLCs (Figure 5E), such as: 'Organelle organization', 'Cellular component organization or biogenesis', 'Microtubule-based process'.
claims.evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The expression levels of multiple epigenetic modifiers were significantly altered in either ESCs or EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: Data shows that the expression levels of multiple epigenetic modifiers were significantly altered, albeit at a low level, in either ESCs or EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure (|log2(fold-change)|>0.25, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The expression levels of the DNA dioxygenase Tet2 were significantly increased in EpiLCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: In particular, the expression levels of the DNA dioxygenase Tet2 were significantly increased in EpiLCs following Δ9-THC exposure, which would contribute to changes in DNA methylation dynamics and differentiation potential (Sohni et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and citation to Sohni et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The expression of the histone deacetylases Hdac5 and Hdac11 were significantly decreased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: The expression of the two histone deacetylases Hdac5 and Hdac11 were significantly decreased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure, while the expression of the histone phosphorylase Rps6ka5 increased under the same conditions.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The expression of the histone phosphorylase Rps6ka5 increased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: The expression of the two histone deacetylases Hdac5 and Hdac11 were significantly decreased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure, while the expression of the histone phosphorylase Rps6ka5 increased under the same conditions.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The expression of the histone methyltransferase Kmt2c was significantly increased in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: In EpiLCs, the expression of the histone methyltransferase Kmt2c and of the regulators of histone ubiquitination Dzip3 and Mysm1 were all significantly increased upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The expression of the regulators of histone ubiquitination Dzip3 and Mysm1 were significantly increased in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: In EpiLCs, the expression of the histone methyltransferase Kmt2c and of the regulators of histone ubiquitination Dzip3 and Mysm1 were all significantly increased upon Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: RNA-seq data suggests the existence of an epigenetic remodelling following Δ9-THC exposure.
claims.source: Collectively, RNA-seq data suggests the existence of an epigenetic remodelling following Δ9-THC exposure, although further analysis of the respective epigenetic marks associated with these modifiers is needed.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing altered expression of epigenetic modifiers.

claims.claim: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, there was a significant decrease in double-negative (DN) cells and a corresponding significant increase in single-positive (SP) and double-positive (DP) PGCLCs.
claims.source: Specifically, at 100 nM Δ9-THC, a significant decrease in DN was observed, with a corresponding significant increase of 1.14-fold in SP and of 1.64-fold in DP cells (Figure 6C, p=0.0002, p=0.05, and p=1.55–06 for 100 nM of Δ9-THC in DN, SP, and DP populations respectively compared to the mock-treated condition, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The same pattern of increased PGCLC induction was observed when male ESCs and EpiLCs exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC were differentiated into PGCLCs.
claims.source: The same pattern was observed when male ESCs and EpiLCs exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC were differentiated in PGCLCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, a smaller proportion of DN cells underwent two or three mitotic divisions compared to the control.
claims.source: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, a smaller proportion of DN cells underwent two or three mitotic divisions compared to the control (Figure 6D, 1.14-fold fewer cells and 1.12-fold fewer cells, p=0.05 and p=0.04 for 2 divisions and 3 divisions, respectively, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by proliferation tracing data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, a significantly higher proportion of SP and DP cells underwent three mitotic divisions compared to the control.
claims.source: In parallel, for the same dose, a significantly higher proportion of SP and DP cells underwent three mitotic divisions compared to the control (Figure 6D, 1.24-fold and 1.11-fold, p=0.03 and p=0.0035, for 3 divisions in SP and DP cells, compared to the control, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by proliferation tracing data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The higher number of PGCLCs observed upon Δ9-THC exposure originates from their increased proliferation during their specification and differentiation.
claims.source: These results, therefore, indicate that the higher number of PGCLCs observed upon Δ9-THC exposure originates from their increased proliferation during their specification and differentiation.
claims.evidence: Supported by proliferation tracing data and inference.

claims.claim: No ∆9-THC could be detected in day 5 embryoid bodies, indicating that ∆9-THC does not persist to levels higher than the limit of detection of mass spectrometry (1 ng/mL).
claims.source: Data shows that no ∆9-THC could be detected in day 5 embryoid bodies, indicating that ∆9-THC does not persist to levels higher than the limit of detection of mass spectrometry (1 ng/mL).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The proliferative effects in PGCLCs are not due to residual ∆9-THC persisting in the cells during differentiation.
claims.source: This suggests that the proliferative effects are not due to residual ∆9-THC persisting in the cells during differentiation towards PGCLCs.
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data showing no detectable ∆9-THC in day 5 embryoid bodies.

claims.claim: Δ9-THC causes an alteration of the developmental kinetics that PGCLCs normally undergo, even in the absence of direct continuous exposure.
claims.source: Thus, Δ9-THC causes an alteration of the developmental kinetics that PGCLCs normally undergo, even in the absence of direct continuous exposure.
claims.evidence: Supported by proliferation and induction efficiency data in PGCLCs derived from exposed precursors.

claims.claim: NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratio in whole day 5 embryoid bodies deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs increased 1.17-fold compared to those deriving from mock-treated cells.
claims.source: First, NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H assessment revealed a modest but significant 1.17-fold increase in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratio in whole day 5 embryoid bodies deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs compared to those deriving from mock-treated cells (Figure 7B, P=0.01, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: A significant increase in mitochondrial membrane potential (MFI) was observed in DN, SP and DP populations deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs compared to those deriving from mock controls.
claims.source: A significant increase in MFI was observed in DN, SP and DP populations deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs compared to those deriving from mock controls (Figure 7C, 1.17, 1.16, 1.23 -fold, p=0.006, p=0.05 and p=0.01 for DN, SP, and DP, respectively, unpaired T-test).
claims.evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The metabolic changes induced by Δ9-THC prior to PGCLCs induction and differentiation are not reset during the profound reprogramming that PGCLCs undergo.
claims.source: These results indicate that the metabolic changes induced by Δ9-THC prior to PGCLCs induction and differentiation are not reset during the profound reprogramming that PGCLCs undergo.
claims.evidence: Supported by metabolic profiling data showing sustained changes in PGCLCs.

claims.claim: PCA of DP PGCLCs transcriptome delineated a transcriptional signature of prior Δ9-THC exposure.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure at physiologically relevant doses (10 nM to 1 µM) significantly increases the proliferation of naive mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) in a dose-dependent manner, as evidenced by increased viable cell numbers, BrdU incorporation, and G2/M phase cells. This proliferative effect is sex-independent and occurs without significant cytotoxicity until the maximal dose of 100 µM.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C30-C35 collectively demonstrate increased ESC proliferation upon Δ9-THC exposure through multiple independent measures (viable cell counts, BrdU incorporation, cell cycle analysis) with appropriate statistical significance (p<0.05) and biological replicates (N=3, n=3). The dose-response relationship is well-characterized, and sex-independence is confirmed in both female and male ESCs.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure does not increase the proliferation of primed pluripotent stem cells (EpiLCs), and at higher doses (10 µM) significantly decreases both viable cell numbers and BrdU incorporation compared to mock-treated conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C36-C38 provide consistent evidence that EpiLCs respond differently than ESCs to Δ9-THC exposure, with no proliferative effect at lower doses and cytotoxic effects at 10 µM. The data are supported by multiple measurements (viability, cell counts, BrdU incorporation) with appropriate statistical testing.

results.result: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), which resemble primed pluripotent cells like mouse EpiLCs, show decreased cell numbers upon Δ9-THC exposure without significant impact on viability at 100 nM.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 demonstrate that hESCs respond similarly to mouse EpiLCs rather than mouse ESCs, supporting the hypothesis that the proliferative response to Δ9-THC is specific to naive pluripotent cells. The data are statistically significant (p=0.004) with appropriate replicates.

results.result: The increased proliferation of ESCs by Δ9-THC is dependent on CB1 receptor binding, as demonstrated by the CB1 antagonist SR141716 abolishing the proliferative effect. However, CB1 expression levels at the cell surface are equivalent between ESCs and EpiLCs, indicating that receptor expression alone does not explain the differential proliferative response.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C42-C44 provide mechanistic insight through pharmacological inhibition (SR141716) and Western blot analysis. The antagonist experiment demonstrates CB1 dependence with strong statistical significance (p=1.66×10⁻⁵), while the Western blot shows equivalent CB1 expression between cell types, ruling out differential receptor expression as the mechanism.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure increases both glycolytic rates and mitochondrial activity in ESCs at 100 nM, as evidenced by increased NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios, mitochondrial membrane potential, maximal glycolytic capacity (ECAR), and maximal respiratory capacity (OCR).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C45, C49, C51, C54 collectively demonstrate metabolic reprogramming in ESCs through multiple complementary assays (WST-1, Mitotracker, Seahorse). The increases are statistically significant and consistent across different metabolic measurements, providing strong evidence for Δ9-THC-induced metabolic changes.

results.result: EpiLCs show increased glycolytic capacity at 100 nM Δ9-THC but no changes in mitochondrial activity or NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios, consistent with their already glycolytic metabolic state. At 10 µM, both glycolytic capacity and NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios significantly decrease.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47, C50-C53, C56 demonstrate that EpiLCs respond differently to Δ9-THC than ESCs, with selective effects on glycolysis but not mitochondrial respiration. The data are consistent with the known metabolic phenotype of primed pluripotent cells and include appropriate statistical testing.

results.result: The increase in maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs at 100 nM Δ9-THC is observed only for maximal capacity, not for basal or ATP-linked respiration, suggesting that Δ9-THC impact on mitochondrial respiration does not support increased energetic production.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 provides important mechanistic insight by distinguishing between different components of mitochondrial respiration. The selective increase in maximal capacity without changes in basal or ATP-linked respiration suggests that the metabolic changes are not primarily for energy production, which is consistent with the anabolic hypothesis.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure increases anabolic capabilities in both ESCs and EpiLCs, as demonstrated by metabolomics showing upregulation of metabolic pathways involved in synthesis of amino acids, nucleotides, NAD(P)+, and fatty acids. In ESCs, 39 of 126 metabolites were significantly upregulated, while in EpiLCs, 95 of 138 metabolites were upregulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C57-C60, C62 are supported by comprehensive metabolomics analysis using mass spectrometry with appropriate normalization and pathway enrichment analysis. The data show consistent upregulation of anabolic pathways in both cell types, with substantial overlap (79.49% of ESC upregulated metabolites also upregulated in EpiLCs).

results.result: The ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione (GSH/GSSG) was unchanged in both ESCs and EpiLCs in response to Δ9-THC, suggesting that increased mitochondrial respiration does not cause overt elevation of oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 provides important negative control data showing that the metabolic changes induced by Δ9-THC do not result in oxidative stress, which could be a confounding factor. The measurement is direct and appropriate for assessing oxidative stress.

results.result: Inhibition of glycolysis by 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG) abrogates the Δ9-THC-induced increase in both ESC cell number and NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H levels, demonstrating that increased glycolysis is necessary for Δ9-THC-induced proliferation in ESCs. While Δ9-THC increases anabolism in both ESCs and EpiLCs, this increased anabolism only supports cellular proliferation in ESCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 provide critical mechanistic evidence through pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis. The 2-DG experiment demonstrates causality between glycolysis and proliferation with strong statistical significance (p=5.56×10⁻⁵ for cell number). The integration of metabolomics and proliferation data across cell types supports the conclusion that anabolism alone is insufficient for proliferation.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure is associated with moderate transcriptomic changes in both ESCs and EpiLCs, with only 12 genes significantly upregulated and 9 downregulated (log2FC >0.5) in ESCs. The vast majority of transcriptome variation is attributed to cell type (98%) rather than Δ9-THC exposure (1%), and Δ9-THC does not appear to influence differentiation dynamics from ESCs to EpiLCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C65-C68 are supported by comprehensive RNA-seq analysis with appropriate PCA and differential expression analysis. The low number of DEGs and the PCA results clearly demonstrate that transcriptional changes are modest compared to metabolic changes, which is a key finding of the study.

results.result: Gene ontology analysis reveals that upregulated genes in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure are enriched for metabolic pathways involved in anabolism, while upregulated genes in EpiLCs are enriched for terms related to alterations in cellular components and organelle organization rather than metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by appropriate GO enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data. The differential GO term enrichment between ESCs and EpiLCs provides mechanistic insight into how transcriptional changes support the observed metabolic and proliferative phenotypes in a cell-type-specific manner.

results.result: The expression levels of multiple epigenetic modifiers were significantly altered in ESCs and EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure, including DNA methylation enzymes (Tet2), histone deacetylases (Hdac5, Hdac11), histone phosphorylases (Rps6ka5), histone methyltransferases (Kmt2c), and regulators of histone ubiquitination (Dzip3, Mysm1), suggesting epigenetic remodeling following Δ9-THC exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 identify changes in expression of epigenetic modifiers from RNA-seq data, but the authors explicitly state that 'further analysis of the respective epigenetic marks associated with these modifiers is needed.' The changes are at low levels (|log2FC|>0.25) and no direct measurements of epigenetic marks (DNA methylation, histone modifications) are provided. The suggestion of epigenetic remodeling is speculative without functional validation.

results.result: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, there is a significant increase in PGCLC induction efficiency (1.64-fold increase in double-positive cells) and proliferation during specification and differentiation, as demonstrated by increased mitotic divisions in single-positive and double-positive populations. This effect is observed in both female and male cells and originates from increased proliferation rather than altered differentiation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by flow cytometry and proliferation tracing data with appropriate statistical significance. The use of fluorescent reporters (Blimp1:mVenus and Stella:CFP) allows precise quantification of PGCLC populations, and the proliferation tracing with CellTrace Yellow provides direct evidence for the mechanism of increased PGCLC numbers.

results.result: No Δ9-THC could be detected in day 5 embryoid bodies by mass spectrometry (detection limit 1 ng/mL), indicating that the proliferative effects in PGCLCs are not due to residual Δ9-THC persisting during differentiation. Thus, Δ9-THC causes an alteration of developmental kinetics that PGCLCs undergo even in the absence of direct continuous exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 provide critical evidence that the effects on PGCLCs represent a 'memory' of prior exposure rather than direct effects of persistent Δ9-THC. The mass spectrometry quantification is appropriate and the detection limit is clearly stated. This supports the concept of metabolic memory as a mechanism.

results.result: A memory of metabolic rewiring by Δ9-THC is retained throughout differentiation to PGCLCs in the absence of direct exposure, as evidenced by increased NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios (1.17-fold) in whole embryoid bodies and increased mitochondrial membrane potential in all PGCLC subpopulations (DN, SP, DP) derived from Δ9-THC-exposed ESCs and EpiLCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C87-C89 demonstrate metabolic memory through direct measurements of metabolic parameters in PGCLCs that were not directly exposed to Δ9-THC. The increases are modest but statistically significant (p<0.05) and consistent across multiple cell populations, supporting the concept of metabolic memory.

results.result: Metabolic memory of Δ9-THC exposure in PGCLCs is associated with an alteration of their transcriptional profile, with PCA showing clear separation by exposure status (PC1=59%, PC2=24%). Most transcriptional changes are toward downregulation (97 genes down vs. 11 up), but upregulated genes are enriched for oxidative phosphorylation processes, indicating that metabolic changes are retained through transcriptional reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C90-C93 are supported by RNA-seq analysis of sorted double-positive PGCLCs with appropriate PCA, differential expression analysis, and GO enrichment. The transcriptional signature of prior exposure is clear, and the enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation genes among upregulated DEGs is consistent with the observed metabolic changes.

results.result: Despite increased PGCLC numbers and mitochondrial activity, the functional annotation of GO terms associated with downregulated genes suggests degradation of PGCLC quality, with enrichment for terms related to structural cellular components, extracellular environment interactions, and cell adhesion and junction.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 are supported by GO enrichment analysis of downregulated genes in PGCLCs. The interpretation that downregulation of structural and adhesion genes suggests 'degradation of quality' is reasonable given the known importance of these processes in PGC development, though direct functional assays of PGCLC quality would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure in ESCs and EpiLCs durably alters their metabolome and these changes are carried through PGCLC specification and differentiation, leading to an alteration of PGCLCs transcriptional program.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 represents the integration of multiple lines of evidence (metabolomics in ESCs/EpiLCs, metabolic profiling in PGCLCs, transcriptomics in PGCLCs) demonstrating that metabolic changes persist across developmental stages. This is the central conclusion of the paper and is well-supported by the comprehensive multi-omics approach.

results.result: The metabolic signatures associated with Δ9-THC exposure in ESCs are reminiscent of those occurring during naive-to-primed transition, with Δ9-THC coaxing ESCs to rely more on aerobic glycolysis and driving anabolic pathways that lead to proliferation. In EpiLCs, the impact of Δ9-THC is not sufficient to override their existing highly proliferative, glycolytic metabolic program.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 represent a mechanistic synthesis of the metabolic and proliferation data, comparing Δ9-THC effects to known developmental metabolic transitions. The comparison is well-supported by the data and provides a conceptual framework for understanding the differential effects in naive vs. primed cells.

results.result: The NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios were slightly but significantly decreased at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in hESCs, in agreement with the deleterious effect of Δ9-THC on cell number.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p=0.04), though the effect is modest (0.09-fold decrease). This finding is consistent with the decreased cell numbers observed in hESCs and supports the hypothesis that primed-like cells respond differently to Δ9-THC than naive cells.

results.result: Background claims establishing the prevalence of cannabis use (49.6 million users in US, 7-12% of pregnant women), the role of Δ9-THC as the primary psychoactive compound acting through CB1 receptors, and the known effects of cannabis exposure on fertility, reproduction, and transgenerational outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C20 are background/context claims supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish the rationale for the study but are not novel findings of this work.

results.result: Background claims establishing the biological context of pluripotent stem cells, their metabolic characteristics, and the developmental biology of primordial germ cells, including their sensitivity to environmental insults.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C29 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide the scientific context for using ESCs, EpiLCs, and PGCLCs as a model system but are not novel findings.

results.result: Discussion claims contextualizing the findings within existing literature on cannabis effects on fertility, the novelty of studying early embryonic stages, the role of CB1 receptors in proliferation, metabolic perturbation by Δ9-THC, the importance of PGC metabolic reprogramming, metabolites as carriers of inheritance, and the utility of in vitro gametogenesis models.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102, C106, C108-C109, C112-C113, C115-C119 are discussion/interpretation claims that contextualize the findings within existing literature. These are appropriately supported by citations and help interpret the significance of the results.

results.result: Interpretive claims concluding that Δ9-THC has lasting consequences on the metabolome of embryonic germ cells in the absence of direct exposure, that metabolic memory is retained during PGCLC differentiation, that downregulated genes suggest degradation of PGCLC homeostasis, that this could impact PGC development in vivo, and that metabolic remodeling may drive exposure memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C107, C110-C111, C114, C122 represent the authors' interpretations and conclusions based on their data. These are well-supported by the experimental evidence, though some aspects (particularly in vivo consequences, C114) remain speculative and would benefit from additional validation.

results.result: Preliminary results in hESCs show that Δ9-THC exposure negatively impacts their global energy metabolism, and future studies will need to confirm whether metabolic reprogramming is also carried over developmental stages in human models for the germline.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 acknowledge that the hESC data are preliminary and that future studies are needed to confirm the findings in human systems. The preliminary data (C120) are supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1, but the authors appropriately recognize the limitations and need for additional work (C121).

results.result: Δ9-THC increases the proliferation of naive mouse ESCs in a dose-dependent manner (from 1 nM to 10 μM), as measured by increased viable cell numbers, BrdU incorporation, and G2/M phase cells. This effect is observed in both female and male ESCs but not in primed EpiLCs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating 'Δ9-THC increases the proliferation rate of mESCs but not mEpiLCs' and noting 'the dose required to cause increased proliferation was approximately 1 nM, which is remarkably low.' The evidence is described as 'convincing' and the proliferation data are accepted without challenge.

results.result: The increased proliferation of ESCs by Δ9-THC is mediated through CB1 receptor signaling, as demonstrated by CB1 antagonist (rimonabant/SR141716) blocking the proliferative effect, despite equal CB1 expression in ESCs and EpiLCs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'Treatment of mESCs with rimonabant (a CB1 receptor antagonist) blocks the effect of 100 nM Δ9-THC on cell proliferation, showing that the proliferative effect is mediated by CB1 receptor signaling.' This mechanistic finding is highlighted as strengthening the study's conclusions.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure increases glycolytic rates, mitochondrial activity (NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios and membrane potential), and anabolic metabolism in ESCs, with metabolomics showing upregulation of pathways for amino acid, nucleotide, and fatty acid synthesis. Glycolysis inhibition by 2-DG blocks the proliferative effect.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these metabolic findings, stating 'treatment with 2-deoxyglucose, a glycolysis inhibitor, also blocks this proliferative effect' and noting 'the effect of Δ9-THC depends on both CB1 signaling and glycolysis.' The metabolomic profiling showing 'broad upregulation of metabolites' and 'upregulation of anabolic genes' is accepted as consistent with increased proliferation.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure causes only moderate transcriptomic changes in ESCs and EpiLCs, with low numbers of differentially expressed genes. In ESCs, upregulated genes are enriched for anabolic metabolic processes, while in EpiLCs, enrichment is for cellular component organization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note 'the transcriptomic changes are modest overall' and state 'there is upregulation of anabolic genes, consistent with the increased proliferation rate in mESCs.' The modest transcriptional impact is accepted as a finding, with no challenges to the interpretation.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure of ESCs and EpiLCs increases PGCLC induction efficiency and proliferation during differentiation, with increased double-positive (DP) PGCLCs and more cell divisions in SP and DP populations, observed in both female and male cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this result, stating 'Δ9-THC treated cells had a moderate increase in the double positive mPGCLC population, and decrease in the double negative population' and 'A cell tracking dye showed that mPGCLCs differentiated from Δ9-THC treated cells had undergone more divisions on average.' The finding is accepted without critique.

results.result: The proliferative effects in PGCLCs are not due to residual Δ9-THC persisting in cells, as mass spectrometry detected no Δ9-THC in day 5 embryoid bodies, indicating Δ9-THC causes lasting alterations in developmental kinetics without direct continuous exposure.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlight this as a key addition to the revised manuscript, stating 'in the revised version, the authors supported their finding of metabolic memory in mPGCLCs by ruling out the potential alternative explanation that Δ9-THC persists in the cultured cells over the course of their experiment.' This addresses a critical alternative explanation.

results.result: A metabolic memory of Δ9-THC exposure is retained in PGCLCs derived from exposed ESCs and EpiLCs, shown by increased NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios and mitochondrial membrane potential in all PGCLC populations, despite the absence of direct exposure during PGCLC differentiation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this central finding, stating 'these effects persist in mESC-derived primordial germ cell-like cells even after Δ9-THC treatment has stopped' and 'mouse primordial germ cell-like cells can have a memory of previous metabolic perturbations.' The metabolic memory concept is accepted as a key contribution.

results.result: PGCLCs derived from Δ9-THC-exposed precursors show altered transcriptional profiles with predominantly downregulated genes enriched for cellular structure, extracellular matrix, and cell adhesion pathways, alongside upregulation of oxidative phosphorylation genes, suggesting both metabolic memory and potential degradation of PGCLC quality.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these transcriptomic findings, noting 'As with the mESCs, these mPGCLCs also had altered gene expression and metabolism, consistent with an increased proliferation rate.' The downregulation of structural and adhesion genes is presented as data without challenge, though reviewers do not extensively discuss the 'quality degradation' interpretation.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure in primed EpiLCs does not increase proliferation or viable cell numbers at physiological doses, and at high doses (10 μM) causes decreased viability and proliferation. EpiLCs show no increase in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios or mitochondrial activity, consistent with their glycolytic metabolism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'Δ9-THC increases the proliferation rate of mESCs but not mEpiLCs' and accept the differential response between cell types. The lack of effect in EpiLCs is treated as an important contrast that helps define the cell-type specificity of Δ9-THC effects.

results.result: Human ESCs (hESCs), which resemble primed pluripotent cells like mouse EpiLCs, show decreased cell numbers and slightly decreased NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios upon Δ9-THC exposure, with preliminary results suggesting negative impacts on energy metabolism.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding but express caution, stating 'it would be premature to conclude that the same effects will be observed in human cells as were observed in mouse cells' and noting these are 'preliminary results.' The data are accepted but their interpretation and generalizability are questioned.

results.result: Δ9-THC exposure alters expression of multiple epigenetic modifiers in ESCs and EpiLCs, including DNA methylation enzymes (Tet2), histone deacetylases (Hdac5, Hdac11), and histone methyltransferases (Kmt2c), suggesting potential epigenetic remodeling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss these epigenetic findings, but they are presented as part of the transcriptomic analysis that reviewers accept. The claim is modest ('suggests') and consistent with the overall acceptance of transcriptomic data, though the functional significance is not validated.

results.result: The GSH/GSSG ratio (reduced to oxidized glutathione) was unchanged in both ESCs and EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure, suggesting that increased mitochondrial respiration does not cause overt oxidative stress.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. It is presented as supporting data for the metabolic characterization and is consistent with the overall metabolic profiling that reviewers accept as 'convincing evidence.'

results.result: This study is the first to investigate Δ9-THC effects on early embryonic developmental stages using an in vitro model, identifying metabolites as carriers of exposure memory across developmental stages and highlighting metabolic remodeling as a driver of exposure memory.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the novelty and significance, stating 'The study is valuable because it shows that physiologically relevant ∆9-THC concentrations have metabolic effects on early mouse embryonic cell types' and 'Potential effects of ∆9-THC exposure during early embryonic development are important for society to understand, and the results of this study are significant for public health.'

results.result: Background claims establishing the prevalence of cannabis use (especially among pregnant women), the psychoactive role of Δ9-THC via CB1 receptors, CB1 expression in reproductive tissues and embryos, and associations between cannabis exposure and reproductive/developmental effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these background claims, which are supported by citations. These contextual claims frame the study's rationale and are implicitly accepted through reviewers' acknowledgment of the study's public health significance.

results.result: Background claims about pluripotent stem cell states, metabolic reprogramming during early development, PGC biology, and the sensitivity of PGCs to environmental insults, establishing the biological context for the experimental model.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these established biological concepts, which are supported by citations. The use of the ESC-EpiLC-PGCLC differentiation model is accepted as appropriate, with reviewers noting it as 'a well-characterized in vitro model.'

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the finding that Δ9-THC increases ESC proliferation but not EpiLC proliferation (C3, C30-C35). OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of statistical methods and replicates, while peer reviewers emphasize the remarkably low effective dose (~1 nM) and describe the evidence as 'convincing.' Both agree the finding is well-supported.

Perfect agreement on CB1 receptor mechanism (C5, C42-C44). Both evaluations support the pharmacological inhibition data with SR141716 and Western blot analysis. OpenEval highlights the strong statistical significance (p=1.66×10⁻⁵), while peer reviewers emphasize this mechanistic finding strengthens the study's conclusions.

Both support metabolic reprogramming in ESCs (C7, C45, C49, C51, C54). OpenEval evaluates multiple complementary assays (WST-1, Mitotracker, Seahorse) with statistical rigor. Peer reviewers group these metabolic findings with glycolysis inhibition data (C63-C64) and metabolomics (C8, C57, C59-C60, C62), accepting the broad metabolic upregulation as consistent with increased proliferation.

OpenEval specifically evaluates glycolysis inhibition experiments (C63-C64) as critical mechanistic evidence with strong statistical significance. Peer reviewers incorporate this finding into their broader metabolic assessment (R3), stating that 2-deoxyglucose blocks proliferation and that effects depend on both CB1 signaling and glycolysis.

OpenEval evaluates metabolomics data (C8, C57-C60, C62) as supported by comprehensive mass spectrometry analysis. Peer reviewers include these metabolomic findings in their broader metabolic assessment, accepting the 'broad upregulation of metabolites' and 'upregulation of anabolic genes' as consistent with increased proliferation.

Both support the finding of modest transcriptional changes (C6, C65-C68). OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive RNA-seq analysis with PCA showing transcriptional changes are modest compared to metabolic changes. Peer reviewers explicitly note 'transcriptomic changes are modest overall' and accept this as a key finding.

Both support GO enrichment analysis findings (C69-C71). OpenEval evaluates the differential GO term enrichment between ESCs and EpiLCs as providing mechanistic insight. Peer reviewers accept the 'upregulation of anabolic genes, consistent with the increased proliferation rate in mESCs.'

Perfect agreement on PGCLC findings (C79-C83). Both evaluations support the increased double-positive PGCLC population and proliferation tracing data. OpenEval emphasizes the flow cytometry methodology and statistical significance, while peer reviewers affirm the moderate increase and accept the finding without critique.

Perfect agreement on Δ9-THC clearance data (C84-C86). Both evaluations support the mass spectrometry evidence ruling out persistent drug as an alternative explanation. OpenEval notes the appropriate detection limit, while peer reviewers highlight this as a key addition to the revised manuscript that addresses a critical alternative explanation.

Both support metabolic memory in PGCLCs (C9, C87-C89). OpenEval evaluates the direct metabolic measurements with modest but significant increases (p<0.05). Peer reviewers affirm this as a central finding, stating 'mouse primordial germ cell-like cells can have a memory of previous metabolic perturbations.'

Both support PGCLC transcriptomic findings (C10, C90-C93). OpenEval evaluates RNA-seq analysis with PCA and GO enrichment showing oxidative phosphorylation upregulation. Peer reviewers accept altered gene expression and metabolism consistent with increased proliferation, though they don't extensively discuss the quality degradation interpretation.

Both support downregulation of structural/adhesion genes in PGCLCs (C94-C97). OpenEval finds the 'degradation of quality' interpretation reasonable but notes functional assays would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers present the data without challenge but don't extensively discuss the quality interpretation.

Both support differential response between ESCs and EpiLCs (C4, C36-C38). OpenEval evaluates consistent evidence of no proliferative effect in EpiLCs at lower doses with cytotoxicity at 10 µM. Peer reviewers accept this as important cell-type specificity, stating 'Δ9-THC increases the proliferation rate of mESCs but not mEpiLCs.'

Both support selective metabolic effects in EpiLCs (C46-C47, C50-C53, C56). OpenEval notes effects on glycolysis but not mitochondrial respiration, consistent with primed cell metabolic phenotype. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their assessment of cell-type-specific responses.

Divergent evaluation certainty. OpenEval supports hESC findings (C39-C41) as statistically significant (p=0.004) and consistent with the hypothesis. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the data but cautioning 'it would be premature to conclude that the same effects will be observed in human cells' and noting these are 'preliminary results.'

OpenEval supports the modest decrease in hESC mitochondrial mass (C48, p=0.04) as consistent with differential response in primed-like cells. Peer reviewers include this in their UNCERTAIN assessment of hESC data, expressing caution about generalizability to human cells.

Both acknowledge limitations of hESC data (C120-C121). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting preliminary data are supported but authors appropriately recognize need for additional work. Peer reviewers similarly express caution about premature conclusions regarding human cells.

Divergent evaluation certainty. OpenEval rates epigenetic modifier findings (C72-C78) as UNCERTAIN, noting low fold-changes and lack of direct epigenetic mark measurements, calling the suggestion 'speculative without functional validation.' Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these as part of the transcriptomic analysis without explicit challenge, though they don't discuss functional significance.

Perfect agreement on oxidative stress data (C61). Both evaluations support this negative control finding. OpenEval notes the measurement is direct and appropriate for assessing oxidative stress. Peer reviewers don't challenge the finding and accept it as supporting data for metabolic characterization.

Both support background/context claims (C1, C11-C20). OpenEval notes these are appropriately cited literature establishing study rationale. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these contextual claims through acknowledgment of the study's public health significance, without challenging the background.

Both support background claims about the model system (C2, C21-C29). OpenEval notes these provide scientific context supported by established literature. Peer reviewers accept the ESC-EpiLC-PGCLC differentiation model as 'a well-characterized in vitro model' without challenge.

Both support discussion/interpretation claims contextualizing findings (C99-C102, C106, C108-C109, C112-C113, C115-C119). OpenEval notes these are appropriately supported by citations. Peer reviewers affirm novelty and significance, stating the study is 'valuable' and 'significant for public health.'

Both support authors' conclusions (C107, C110-C111, C114, C122). OpenEval notes these are well-supported by experimental evidence though some aspects remain speculative. Peer reviewers affirm the significance for public health and society's need to understand potential effects of Δ9-THC exposure.

OpenEval specifically evaluates the integration of metabolic memory evidence (C98) as the central conclusion well-supported by multi-omics approach. Peer reviewers incorporate this into their broader assessment of PGCLC findings, accepting that metabolic and transcriptional changes persist.

OpenEval supports the mechanistic synthesis comparing Δ9-THC effects to developmental metabolic transitions (C103-C105). Peer reviewers incorporate the cell-type specificity concept (C105) into their assessment of differential responses between ESCs and EpiLCs.

OpenEval supports the distinction between mitochondrial respiration components (C55), noting selective increase in maximal capacity without changes in basal or ATP-linked respiration supports the anabolic hypothesis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific mechanistic detail.
